status_reasoning: Reviewers describe this as 'a very nice description of a remarkable new finding' and state that 'the results are outstanding.' They explicitly note 'a large difference in bacterial growth was observed, and a four to five fold difference in embryo survival was observed upon injection with bacteria.' The core finding that histones on lipid droplets kill bacteria in Drosophila embryos is accepted without challenge to its validity.

Reviewers express concern that 'as of now the effect has been seen only in early embryos and not in adult flies' and request discussion of 'whether this might apply to the adult organism.' They note this as 'an important limitation that needs to be addressed' and ask for clarification about whether adult Jabba flies are compromised. While not rejecting the adult fly data presented, reviewers indicate the evidence is insufficient to conclude the system functions broadly in adults.

Reviewers raise 'some issues regarding the experiments using mammalian cell lines,' noting that 'measuring the efficiency of an LPS infection is usually defined by cytokine response rather than hepatic injury' and suggesting bacterial killing assays with intracellular bacteria would strengthen claims. They recommend to 'tone down this section as well because the experiments presented are also rather limited, if provocative.' The mammalian data is characterized as interesting but insufficient.

The reviewers do not challenge the mechanistic finding that LPS and LTA trigger histone release from lipid droplets. This mechanism is implicitly accepted as part of the 'remarkable new finding' and is not mentioned as requiring additional validation or modification. The lack of critique suggests reviewer acceptance of this mechanistic component.

Reviewers 'recommend that the effect of Jabba be tested in another mutant background (jabba/deficiency) to exclude a possible background effect.' This indicates concern about whether the observed phenotypes are definitively attributable to Jabba loss rather than potential secondary mutations. While the two independent alleles provide some confidence, reviewers want additional genetic validation before fully supporting the genetic interpretation.
